To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

PKC and cAMP promote the rapid formation in Aplysial bag cell neuron endings of new sites of Ca2+ influx that are associated with a change of neurite morphology and that are likely to contribute to the potentiated release of peptide neurotransmitters.

PKC and cyclic AMP promote the rapid formation and movement of secretory vesicles in the Aplysia nervous system, and that these processes are associated with the formation of new calcium influx sites at the leading edge.
activation of protein kinase C and cyclic AMP causes the formation of morphological specializations that promote peptide release.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of the release of neuropeptides in the bag cell neurons of Aplysia.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the formation and potentiation of synapses and other forms of intercellular communication in the nervous system.
the regulation of neuropeptide release by intracellular second messengers and by extracellular signals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PKC activation promotes the rapid appearance, at the distal end of the lamellapodia, of new sites of voltage-dependent Ca2+ influx.

the activation of PKC and cAMP in Aplysias bag cell neurons leads to the formation of new sites of Ca2+ influx associated with a morphological change of growth cone endings, and this change promotes the movement of secretory granules to the new sites.
PKC and cAMP are both involved in the regulation of the formation of new sites of Ca2+ influx and that this regulation may be involved in the potentiation of neuropeptide release.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PKC and cyclic AMP promote the rapid formation and movement of secretory vesicles to sites of calcium influx, which are formed by the PKC-dependent extension of neurite endings.
PKC and cAMP promote the rapid formation and movement of putative neurosecretory sites.

the rapid formation of new release sites involves a cascade of intracellular signaling events, including activation of the protein kinase C, recruitment of calcium channels, and the movement of secretory granules.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PKC and cAMP act in concert to promote the rapid formation and potentiation of neuropeptide release.
the activation of PKC and cAMP can promote the formation of new release sites in a matter of minutes, and that this process involves the recruitment of calcium channels to the new sites.
PKC and cAMP can rapidly remodel neurites and that this remodeling is associated with the formation of new release sites.
